utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court, could I please have two minutes in private session? I would like to finish with the story about the witness that the Prosecutor started yesterday, the witness who allegedly was in the courtroom following the proceedings on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you can do it, but would you do it quickly, because we must get on with the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we could have the witness too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the witness is coming in, can I explain to the Court that there are a few documents to put to this witness. I'll try and deal with other matters, if his memory isn't complete, by showing him documents that don't have to be exhibited. But the Chamber may be comforted by the knowledge, I think, from what we are told, that this is the last of the witnesses dealing with these areas which are likely to be the more document-heavy areas, and that after that, I should think there's much less chance of documents having to be produced at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have before him an existing exhibit that we've looked at, 372.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, we are going to leave the early part of 1993, but for completeness, before we do so, I would like your comments on a document produced by Dzemal Merdan. We, that is, the Judges and counsel, have seen the document before, but it wasn't very -- it wasn't dealt with in great detail, and I would like your comments on it. You will remember, Major, that we were looking yesterday at documents from the International Community at about the same time as this 17th of January document which you have, on this occasion, in a language which you understand and that we can have and the usher can very kindly place on the ELMO, please, in English. What I would like your help with first is that this refers to a commission for negotiations to resolve the conflict in Gornji Vakuf and is dated either the 16th or the 17th of January. Can you remember anything about that commission?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I please read the document first, if possible, and then I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a long document, but I'm happy for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, would you like to take him to the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll see the heading refers to the commission for negotiations to resolve the conflict as early as the 16th of January. Do you recall that such a commission was established at an early stage?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first paragraph, he refers to intermittent artillery fire, less intense than on the previous day, and the surrounding villages of Voljevac, Here, and Pridvorci being shelled because of the movement of their troops being detected. Is that correct? Did you shell those villages?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The range of the artillery that I had available could not have reached those villages. If there was any kind of shelling or any conflicts between the HVO and the Muslim army, then it only could have been from Rama Prozor, the neighbouring municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this is an internal document. It's from Merdan to the chiefs of the supreme staff of the RBH armed forces. And that's his account. And then at the next paragraph he speaks how at 1750 hours Colonels Andric and Siljeg arrived, having been at Prozor to discuss matters with Praljak, accompanied by Lucic. And during the meeting they set forth their demands, which were for organisation of the provinces being temporary, based on reciprocity. If there were changes in Geneva, the Croats would abide by the changes. HVO demanded withdrawal of units, return of units, to places from where they set out. They guaranteed they would do nothing against Muslims who had not perpetrated war crimes. They said they'd respect equality, and there was an order to abandon trenches and the army could no longer be commanded by Topcic, Agic, or Prijic, and so on. Now, I just want to know: Is what it set out there by way of the HVO terms the reality?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not a member of this commission. I cannot give any answers concerning the work of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop now, because the point I want to make is an obvious one. This is an internal document, Muslim to Muslim. Now -- not intended for your sight. Have you read so far, please, anything in this document that you say is false, or is it all thus far true?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. All negotiations and discussions -- I can say the following in connection with all of that. A ceasefire was agreed that was fully respected by the HVO. During these ceasefires, there was frequent sniper fire where we lost more soldiers than in the actual fighting. That is to say that the Muslim side did sign most documents, but they did not abide by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question. The question is: Is there anything in the document, which has been read to you so far, that is, which is false or not true, or can you not say?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that this is a document of the commander of the Muslim army to the Muslim units that were operating in the area, and I cannot speak about a document that does not relate to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can, Mr. Sekerija. Just think. You are being asked whether the terms which are represented in the documents as being the terms of the HVO were in fact those terms or not, or are you not in a position to say?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position, Major, is that you're going to deny knowledge of anything that you find is embarrassing for your cause, and it's as simple as that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from a witness Williams, from the International Community, that Colonel Andric gave an ultimatum to the ABiH to hand over their weapons on the basis that Gornji Vakuf was in a Croat canton. Now, did Colonel Andric give that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I was not present at such negotiations at UN headquarters in Vakuf and I indeed cannot speak about that. I personally have not had any document about this in my own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to go back for 1992 and I'll finish with the latter part of 1993. You joined the HVO in April 1992. You speak of Kordic advocating 50 per cent of weapons to go to Muslims. Well, which particular set of weapons was he making this proposal for?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exclusively a question of weapons that were taken over from the former barracks of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and these were small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was he not so much advocating a division as pleading to get some weapons for himself? Is that the reality of the position?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have to plead with anyone, because the HVO units that were under HVO-held territory took those weapons, so he didn't really have to plead with anybody for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is this documented, this offer of his, as you would have it, that 50 per cent of the weapons should go to -- who is it? The Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting where I was present once, where all the presidents of governments within the zone of responsibility of Central Bosnia, where logistic support was being discussed to units on the ground, and at the front line, that is, I think that on several occasions equipment that was in the territory of one municipality that had an abundance of it would go to those municipalities where there was a shortage. Mr. Kordic also advocated a half/half division. If we had, for example, a thousand guns, he asked that half of this be given to the Muslims and half to the Croats, depending on the needs expressed by various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've one more chance, and I'll move on. Can you tell me, please, where I can find or where we can find documents to support what you're saying about this?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had a diary of my own where I made such an entry. After I was injured, my vehicle disappeared and my documents and everything, so I made this kind of an entry in this diary that I had. I cannot find another document to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now at this time, April and May of 1992, what legitimacy did the HVO have, please? You were a member of it. What legitimacy did it have, what right did it have, to have arms from the former Yugoslavia? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't have any right to do it, but what we seized from the barracks of the former JNA is what we had and what we distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were you doing something that was truly dedicated to the continuation of the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina or were you doing something that was aimed at the interests of wider Croatia, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I exclusively did all my work in the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it is my one and only homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2360.18, please. Original for the witness, English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you had already joined the HVO, you were a couple of months into it, at the time Bobetko from the Republic of Croatia set out in this document that he was forming or there was to be formed an IZM for Central Bosnia, with the aim of organising effective defence and integrating the existing commands in Central Bosnia. He ordered the establishment of an IZM, Central Bosnia, in Gornji Vakuf. Can you explain, please, to the Judges how it came about that the State of Croatia at this time was involved in doing what it was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Brigadier Zarko Tole came to the area of Uskoplje, this order, that was signed by General Bobetko that you just showed me now, I see for the first time now. I don't know what kind of political line this is and who this was agreed with, but it is true that Brigadier Tole managed to come to Uskoplje and he did try to organise units there until he was taken by the Serbs. And as for the rest, I already said that in my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Judges that you there, in Gornji Vakuf, about which you give evidence, had no knowledge that the appointments of Tole were being ordered from Croatia? Do you have no knowledge of that at all, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that this is the first time I see this order. Tole came under the orders of the late Mate Boban to set this up probably through political structures at top level, as this was agreed both with the Muslim and the Croat sides. It is possible that this exists. This is the first time I see this document. I cannot discuss it, because it is not my document, and I did not sign it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you were there. Now, was what you were doing related to the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina or was it, to your knowledge, related to the interests of Croatia and dominated by instructions coming from Croatia, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I worked in the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina alone, only, and this is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move from this period of time, the time when Kordic was engaged in offering 50 per cent of the weapons, as you say, to the Muslims, can you explain again -- you answered one of the Judges about this yesterday -- can you explain again, please, how it is that Kordic dealing with allocation of weapons is not a military function?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in any country the government of a country or the presidency of a country are responsible for the logistical supply of the army. Mr. Kordic -- and I affirm that once again he had no command authority to issue orders to units on the front line, nor did he participate in the design of the strategy in the territory that we kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Logistics is a function of a politician because -- or at least to this extent: the politicians may have to find the money to buy the guns, and that may be dealt with by a president, or prime minister, or, I suppose, a minister of war. Now, the logistical functions that you're referring to here, are those, as it were, the political functions of somebody like a minister for war or a minister for defence; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think all the political functions of a government, yes, indeed, all those functions are political and they are not military. And even if we talk about the Minister of Defence, it is once again a political function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence is plainly more closely associated with war than, for example, the Minister of Social Security or the Minister for Education. Is there any politician that you can name who was more closely associated with the political functions of defence than Kordic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the Croat Defence Council was Mate Boban, as one can see from the rules of the armed forces of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, which he signed with his own hand. Then the link between the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HVO and the government was the president of the government or the prime minister, that is, Jadranko Prlic, who held that post at the time. And in his government, there was the Ministry of Defence, which was the link with the Main Staff of the HVO. And the Main Staff of the HVO issued orders, that is, military orders, about the deployment of forces on the ground, their commands to the commanders of the operative zones, and then they transmitted those orders to brigades and other subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, with such a complete chain of political responsibility for military matters, why would it be necessary for Kordic to be negotiating over the allocation of weapons? Why didn't he leave it to Prlic or Boban?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just explained that Mr. Kordic was a vice-president of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, and he was responsible -- presumably he was responsible for the area of Central Bosnia regarding the logistical support on behalf of the Minister of Defence. But I repeat, he had nothing to do with the military command, or if he did anything to do with it, then it was limited to logistical support through the presidents of individual local governments which were in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll discuss that further with the witness. As a matter of record, do you accept -- I have the document, if you need it to confirm it, but as a matter of record and for purposes of dates, that Blaskic appointed you on the 4th of July as commander of Operative Zone Number 1, which covered Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica, Kaonik, Kupres and Prozor. Do you accept that date?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I know the order that you are referring to, since I was at that time Colonel Blaskic's deputy. Then we divided Operative Zone Central Bosnia into four subzones. In one of them, I was the commander, and the duty that I was supposed to carry out was performed by Vlado Bandic until the late Baldo [phoen] Strujic was appointed to that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one document I will come back to out of sequence in a second in order to deal with things swiftly. May the witness see, please, Exhibit 207, which is a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is a document. You have the original. The English version is on the ELMO. It doesn't have a date, but it's in the hand of, apparently, and signed by Dario Kordic, with a stamp for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It reads: "Tiho and Sekerija". That would appear to be you; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says that: "Mr. Franjo Masusa, a HOS commander from Novi Travnik, has been to see me, and that they have decided that a platoon of 30 troops should go to Jajce. Organise other people from other municipalities. I have prepared three lorry loads of supplies so that everything goes together." The same question, please, Major. I know your answer will be that this is not a military order. Can you please tell the Judges why it's not a military order?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there is an established system as applied in Central Bosnia regarding the participation of all the units in defence of Jajce against Bosnian Serbs. And that system said as follows: Every municipality in our area of responsibility would give 20, 30, 35 men, depending on the number, and all those men would come together and go to the front in Jajce. And it says also here, very nicely, that a HOS platoon will also go. It was not under the direct command of the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia that it would come with us, but that we should ensure three lorry loads of medicines, food and fuel to go with them, because there were just too many Chetnik shells there and that was the only surplus. Everything else was in short supply. So, Your Honours, I simply do not agree that this is a military order. This is merely a request to find somewhere three lorries in order to take food, medicines and fuel, which was in short supply on that front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first thing is that the first sentence, or the first clause of the second paragraph, says, "organise other people from other municipalities," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps nothing to do, on its face, with medicine or supplies. It appears to be other armed people from other municipalities. It doesn't bear any other interpretation, does it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but I already told you that it was already a well-established system, that the units in the area of our responsibility took shifts every two or three weeks; some would come back and others go to the ground, and we used the same lorries to bring those back and take those out. The roads there were very difficult. We had to -- routes were dangerous. We had to use macadam roads at night, without any lights whatsoever. So these vehicles that Mr. Kordic is talking about, three lorries of medicines and food -- and I do remember well the duties about food and some fuel for generators, because there was no power there to organise that and to take it there, because such a convoy could not be sent in that direction without proper escort. And in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, I'm not going to cut your answers off if you think they're helpful and responsive to the question, but please focus on the question. "Organise other people from other municipalities," it's a military instruction, and it hasn't been necessary for Kordic to go via Blaskic, it hasn't been necessary for him to go up to the Ministry of Defence. He gives the instruction himself. This is a military instruction; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that it was a well-established system. What was he intending to organise with? Well, we were already organised. He could have written anything he liked at that time, but he could not order anyone to go and get killed in Sumarija, because he was not a part of the chain of command in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I part from this document, can you think of any good reason, please, why this order comes from him and not from someone in the military chain of command like Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier -- Sorry, Mr. Nice. I just wanted to ask a question. After you received this communication from Mr. Kordic, did you have the other people organised, the other people from the other municipalities organised, following receipt of this communication?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this -- Your Honours, this had all been done before. I told you that it was a system which we had been using for months by then. And, for instance, I am giving an example: In July 1992 you will send so many men every week. There is such an order, and it was sent out to all the units by the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Here it says "organise other people," but they were already organised, so that this document is only -- tells me only what it does say: Prepare three lorry loads so that you can send in some assistance, in medicines and food and fuel. And all the rest had already been done before. I didn't need anything else. And I do have this document, and I do not really see it as an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by you of the people following receipt of the document, irrespective of whether you might have done it before. What I'm asking is whether, having received this document from Mr. Kordic, you went ahead and organised people from other municipalities, irrespective of whether it is something that you would have done and did do before.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before this document, I had already written an order and sent it to municipalities which were to send 30 men to prepare, 30 men, each fully equipped to go to the front line in Jajce. I had also provided three lorries to take this assistance that is referred to. Yes, I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And somewhere in the archive, no doubt, there will be a reply you will have sent to this important vice-president confirming that, as it happened, what he was asking you to do had already been done. Is that your position, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall now. If you really want me to answer about this letter, then we need to have some reference number, a date or something else. This to me is a piece of paper, rather than an order about which I can give you an answer. How can I answer if it says here Luka and Tiho? There is no reference number or anything. How can I refer to this document? So I do not think that there will be a report in the archive or any document to show that I had replied to this, at least as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive me, Major, but when His Honour Judge Robinson was asking you about the second paragraph, you seemed to have detailed recollection of having already made the arrangements that were requested of you or ordered of you there. Would that be wrong? You don't have detailed recollection of what you spoke about in answer to Judge Robinson? Which is it, detailed recollection or no detailed recollection?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Your Honours, if you are addressing me with my rank, then I should be addressed with the rank I truly have, but I much prefer to be addressed as "sir". Now, I have already said that it was a well-established procedure, that I do remember some details and some details I do not recall. I recall it being told that we would get three lorry loads of this, because that was a major assistance for Jajce. And I should also like to mention that decent food and medicines and fuel were distributed amongst the Croats and Muslims in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Thank you for that, and I'm sorry not to have been referring to you by your rank in which you retired, a brigadier, and of course I'll do so. One of the things you say, with the authority of your experience, Brigadier, is that there were criminals acting in their own self-interest. You haven't yet identified who these criminals were. Before we come to that, we've also heard from other witnesses of various special units, PPNs, I think. Now, who are you referring to when you speak of criminals acting in their own self-interest?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about 1992 and the time I spent in the territory of Central Bosnia until I went back to my native municipality for reasons of health, then, Your Honours, I can say that individuals were indeed criminals, and they committed criminal offences in their own self-interest, not only in one municipality; in all municipalities. I call them local sheriffs, who refused to be subordinated, to place themselves under the command of the HVO or any other institutions that existed at the time. And all the plunder or whatever they did, they did only for their personal gain, and in this manner they did a disservice to the Croat people, to the interests of the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, are these individuals different from, for example, the special units, the PPNs, or are you saying that the PPNs were the people acting illegally and out of control?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: During my stay in 1992 in the territory of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia, no special purpose units were formed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when they were formed, to your knowledge, they were under the command of the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because if we look at another new exhibit, which I'm afraid we have no translation, but it's a short exhibit, and it's going to be 179.1. The translation must follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's no good giving it to us unless it's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not to be exhibited unless it's properly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, but I think that the witness can help us materially, and the document, to a large degree, speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at this document, if you look at the stamp on the top, it's hard to read, but it would appear to be the 8th of August of 1992. It's a typed document coming from you, and if we look at item number 4 -- perhaps you'd just like to read item number 4 out in your own language, and then it will be translated for us, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Units of the Vitez HVO Special Purpose Unit is to be ready for engagement along the Vitez-Busovaca-Kiseljak line and to report to the HVO-Kiseljak command."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So is it right, as I would suggest this document shows, that as early as August of 1992, clear command -- clear lines of command for special purpose units from Central Bosnia Operative Zone were known of and operated, including by yourself?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a military police platoon. I recall that event. I recall that this was a military police unit. It was to clear the road and remove all the obstacles along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My general point remains. The special units, as you refer to them generally in that order, were under Central Bosnian control, and there's no evidence that you can point to, or no suggestion that you point to, that the special units were other than under Central Operative Zone control.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I agree with you. I do agree with you. These units were. The military police was under the command of the staff of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. But I did not say that they were engaged, involved, in some nefarious deeds. Those were individuals, or groups of individuals, at least, during my stay in the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to trouble you with another exhibit, but will you confirm -- I've got an exhibit to look at if you want to, but would you confirm that where an anti-aircraft gun was being moved, one that had been first of all moved by you and then was being moved again because Blaskic thought it should be returned to Kresevo, where that happened, the movements of the gun would be well documented. In this case it was a document on the 5th of October of 1992. Do you understand the point? Movements of heavy artillery would always be well documented on paper. You accept that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I needn't trouble you with any exhibit. Exhibit 248, however, a document of yours that I'd like you to look at. This is a document -- you have the original. The English version on the ELMO -- dated the 23rd of October of 1992. It goes to the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Vitez and Busovaca, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and to Dario Kordic. Just before we go on, why are you sending it to the two of them? This isn't being sent to separate addresses so that one can provide a copy to the other; it's being sent to both of them at the same address. Please, why?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained, Your Honours, that the communications that we had at our disposal at that time were not really adequately suited to our needs, and this is merely a letter, or rather an order of the main staff, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, who orders, in military terms, the following to the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. He presumably could not get it. This cable reached Uskoplje, that is, Gornji Vakuf, that is, me. I was there on a sick leave. And I simply rewrote that letter. And I did get some rumours that Blaskic or Kordic had been captured, and I was glad to hear that it was just a false rumour, and that is what I mention in this letter. Likewise, if I may, Your Honours, I should like to say the following: I say here that the situation in the territory of Gornji Vakuf is tense, but nevertheless is still under control. And yesterday I said that even in October 1992 was really a question of whether the conflict -- there would be a conflict or there wouldn't be, and the conflict was hanging in the air. So that all the matters concerning transport or materiel sent towards Novi Travnik, all such convoys are blocked precisely because of the units which are not under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question was about why you sent it to both of them. Your earlier explanation yesterday about needing one to provide the copy to the other won't do, because you're sending it to the same address. If we look at it in detail, it replies to a telegram. Is this an example where you have a recollection of the detail of the telegram or where you don't? Do you recall the telegram? Nobody will criticise you for not recalling it this time after the event, and don't feel pressured to remember it. Just tell us, do you remember the telegram?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would appear from the letter that you're doing two things. In the first part, you're replying to the telegram and you're saying the situation is tense, transports going in the direction of Novi Travnik are blocked. That's a general report on the military position in Gornji Vakuf, and you're sending that to Blaskic and Kordic. Why to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that in case Blaskic does not get it, then we -- then it might go through Mr. Kordic's fax, who can have easier access to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... your only explanation for sending this letter to Kordic, is it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I respectfully suggest to you that that's nonsense, Brigadier, and you know perfectly well you were sending this letter because he was a man with military authority and military interest, and you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I waited for the interpretation. With all due respect, but this is once again a comment of the Prosecutor. He comments on the witness's statements. I do not think one needs to go into argument before witnesses. Arguments should be left for the end. Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a perfectly proper question, because the explanation which is given is that this document was being sent to Mr. Kordic in case it did not get through to Colonel Blaskic. The Prosecution are entitled to put that the real reason for sending the document was because Mr. Kordic had military authority. Now, the Prosecution are entitled to put that as a question, and the witness is entitled to answer. Now, is there anything you would like to say about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know which time this is that I'm saying here that Mr. Dario Kordic never issued military orders either to me or to my subordinates. That is the core of the matter. Never. I came here to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The Prosecutor obviously doesn't seem to be pleased that I'm not speaking the way he would like me to speak. I'm explaining this for five times now, and I'm explaining things the way they actually happened. As for this letter, 248, I assert that I acted in a way which would ensure that Mr. Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic, would get the letter as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. General Sekerija, while you say it's only because it was easier to do it, but I would like to put this question to you: Obviously, this communication is sent to somebody. Is it not sent to Mr. Kordic because he's one of the main people in charge within the HZ HB? After all, it's not just a mailbox, he is a person and an important person. Are you not informing him as a person with responsibility in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, by way of information, yes. But to submit a report to him on military matters, that, no, not under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the distinction? What kind of information would you send to him? What is the difference to be made between military things and what is, in fact, part and parcel of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say this, Your Honour: If there was anyone who was supposed to report to Mr. Kordic about this situation, about political tensions in town, et cetera, it was the president of the local government, that is to say, the head of the local municipality. The president of the local government could have received information from me, and then he could have sent it further up along the line of political responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you admit that Mr. Kordic, as a person with responsibility in the HZ HB, must be informed of the way the situation would develop on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not by the military; rather by the political people, the political structures in the territory of the municipality where something was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your answers, you do not accept at all, if I understand it, that Kordic had any even remote possibility of being involved in military matters; would that be correct? I don't want to overstate your position. Kordic didn't have even the remote possibility of being involved in military matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he been involved in military matters, well, it depends which ones. As for the logistic supply of manpower for units, yes, I agree, he was involved in that. But as for giving orders to units is concerned, assigning tasks to them, I state with full responsibility that he had no possibility of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 249, please. This is five days -- I beg your pardon, no. This is one day after the letter and order that you've sent, and you, I think, were what, number 3 in the hierarchy of Central Bosnia? Would that be about right, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was formed, I was a chief of staff of that Operative Zone, in a military sense, or deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would have to know what was going on, for example, if Bugojno was going to be shelled, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry? Would you like me to repeat the question? You would have to know what was going on if Bugojno was going to be shelled, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, but I already mentioned that as I was wounded at the Jajce front line, when this document was written I was at home, I was on sick leave, I was recuperating. And this was written on the 23rd of October. Therefore, I cannot discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document that we looked at was dated the 23rd of October. This document, according to the handwritten receipt, is sent on the 23rd or the 24th of October. So you still appear to be in the office. And it says: "Information that a unit of the BH army is moving Bugojno," and so on. "Should these units participate in the fighting, we shall use long-range artillery on Bugojno," a deadline, and it's signed by -- the first signature, Dario Kordic, and the second signature, Colonel Blaskic. Now, you were there. Why is Kordic signing an order like this, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, Your Honours. At the end of September, I was wounded at the Jajce front line, and it says very nicely in my CV that I was on sick leave for a month and a half or two. Mr. Prosecutor, at that time I was not in the area of Central Bosnia. I do not wish to speak about a document that was signed by someone else involving something that I was not a participant in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think there may be an explanation. We needn't pursue this, but according to my note, you said that you were wounded in 1993. These documents are, in fact, 1992, and that may be the explanation.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, here in one of the points -- let me just find it. Point number 15 says I worked for Zarko Tole and his successors as HVO Chief of Staff in the Operative Zone Central Bosnia from May of 1992 until early January 1993 for a period of about one month. Beginning on September 23rd, 1992, I was in the hospital, recovering from an injury which I sustained at the Jajce front line. I was wounded on the 4th of August, 1992, and since then I have permanently become a disabled person to a very large extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was not clear, then, from your evidence that it was 1992 that you were talking about. However, we now have it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if that's right, Brigadier, you must have recovered by the 23rd of October, when you were signing the document we've already looked at and which you haven't challenged as being yours, but goes to both Blaskic and Kordic about the situation in Gornji Vakuf. So you had recovered by the 23rd, and therefore you were in a position to know about what was happening on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat. I was in the area of Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, that is, at my own home. I still had plaster on, because I was still at home, still recovering. An order signed by Milivoj Petkovic had reached us because it could not go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please look once more, then, at Exhibit 248 just for this point, because this is actually a signed order, Brigadier, and we've got a copy of your signature on your proof of evidence. The signature on Exhibit 248 is your signature, and you were working on the 23rd of October. So whatever ill health you had suffered and whatever injury you had suffered, you were back at work on the 23rd; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I was in Gornji Vakuf, and I stopped by the brigade of Ante Starcevic every now and then that was stationed in Jajce. I was not in Central Bosnia. And it says nicely here, "Municipal Staff of Gornji Vakuf," that that's where I was, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. How would you -- can he look at Exhibit 261, please. It's the last of the exhibits for 1992 I'm going to ask you to look at. This is an order dated the 29th of October, dealing with Jajce -- so wherever you were, it's something you would have had an interest -- signed by Ivica Rajic, and it says, on the 29th of October: "We received an invitation from the deputy commander, Dario Kordic, deputy commander of the HZ HB." I hope the translation is correct. Would you accept that that's the word that's used?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expression is wrong. It was supposed to say "Vice-President of the HZ HB". I think that this must be a typo, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it goes on to say that: "Based on an order of the chief of the General Staff of the HVO, Petkovic, to send to Jajce immediately all available forces and all available materiel." And Ivica Rajic goes on to stress that this is the final call for Croats and real fighters to save the city and the people, and he therefore issues an order pursuant to Kordic's request. Just your explanation. You were there -- not necessarily here, but your explanation as to whether this shows Kordic doing something that's military or not.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to comment on a document that does not pertain to me. However, there is one thing I wish to say. Your Honours, we know that at the end of October 1992, the town of Jajce had fallen, where about 15 or 17 thousand Croats had lived -- the same number of Muslims as well -- and they all got out. This is a normal document, in my opinion, for any man or any politician calling upon all to go and try to get the people of Jajce out, Croats and Muslims. I don't see anything bad in this. However, I wish to delineate this from what I said, that is to say, this does not pertain to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't want to comment on that. Fine. You're here to testify, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. You've already stated that Mr. Kordic -- you said that -- previously you said that Mr. Kordic was not in the chain of command. Now, does this document not show that Mr. Kordic is well in the chain of command, or how do you view this document in relation to the issue of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I view this document in the following way: "Let us all rally together and let us save what can be saved," because Jajce fell at the end of October. This is a call upon all Croats. Often we had to traverse very tough mountains in order to get all these people out, regardless of their religious or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're not answering the question that the Prosecutor and myself put to you. It is your right. So if you decide not to answer that question, we take due note of the fact that you do not want to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move now, as swiftly as I can, beyond the passage of time I dealt with yesterday at the beginning of -- one or two other questions on '92 and then I'm done. Kordic was called a colonel. Why?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Central Bosnia, and I said quite a few times what this period was while I was there, I personally never addressed Mr. Kordic by his rank. I addressed him as "Mr. Kordic", because I was not aware of this rank of his. Afterwards, I heard that this rank was conferred upon him in haste allegedly because of some negotiations in Sarajevo. However, during my stay there, Mr. Kordic never had a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the important negotiations in Sarajevo, they were important, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were about military matters, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Political and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So how could he deal with the military side of things, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that I heard that he had been at these negotiations. I don't know whether he was there. But please do not trouble me with such questions any longer. I already said that during my stay there, he never had a rank, I never addressed him by this rank, and I heard later that allegedly he got some kind of a rank from Mate Boban and some piece of paper. That's what I heard -- but that's not what I'm asserting -- because of some kind of negotiations that were held at a higher level in Sarajevo. That's the only thing I know about Dario Kordic's rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why was he promoted to brigadier, then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your promotion to brigadier is a genuine promotion, reflecting your military ability, presumably?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1993, you had been moved from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to Gornji Vakuf. As a matter of interest, you now call Gornji Vakuf by another name, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the Turks came to this area, Uskoplje, which is the name that is used today also in the area where Croats lived, was called Uskoplje. When the Turks came, this name was abolished in 1670 something. Don't take my word for it; I'm not very good at history. Uskoplje was abolished, and this town of mine got the name of Gornji Vakuf. The word "Vakuf" itself is a Turkish word, and it reflects religious heritage or something like that. I'm not very good at interpreting things like this. When the war broke out in '93 and later, the Croats of Uskoplje, by way of referendum, decided that this town should be called Uskoplje. Another fact is interesting. In this town, only one election was held. The first multi-party elections were the only ones that were carried through. After that, there were elections that were held, but the results were never carried through. These are -- this is a town that has two names, that has two populations, and that is divided between two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when the name Uskoplje was adopted, it was adopted without referendum, without reference to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the referendum was held amongst the Croat part of the population in terms of changing the name from Gornji Vakuf to Uskoplje. The municipal government of the municipality, that was not functioning legitimately yet within Bosnia-Herzegovina, submitted a request in 1996 for this name to be adopted. To the best of my knowledge, this could be approved by the beginning of August this year, that Uskoplje definitely be established as a newly formed municipality in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1993, I think your evidence would be in summary that there was no use of HV troops from Croatia in your area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From January 1993 until the 4th of August, 1993, when I was wounded, taken to hospital, I assert that the Croat army was never used in this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the time problems, I'm not going to take the witness through the various documents in the international armed conflict binder and elsewhere that are already in evidence. I can provide the Chamber or my friends opposite various numbers that I could ask about. I'll confine myself to dealing with two documents that are outstanding, and then they'll be part of an overall library of documents for this area and for the international armed conflict issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you look, please, first, at a new document, 2404.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one may actually be in the IAC, but I'm going to ask the witness to deal with it in any event. And there's one outstanding Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is dated the 22nd of February of 1993, as you can see. It comes from Zrinko Tokic. It goes to the 4th Brigade in Split, and it says: "Further to your inquiry regarding the death of your combatant, Stanko Posovac, son of Franjo, and from Gornji Vakuf, it was established that Stanko Posovac took part in the fighting between the so-called BH army and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, was wounded by a sniper bullet on the 13th of January, transferred to hospital, died, buried." Your combatant, Stanko Posovac, in a report to the 4th Brigade of the Drazevac barracks in Split. Please explain, if you're sticking to your evidence that the HV made no contribution.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my report, I already said that there were individuals, not some organised unit of the HVO that was fighting in the area of Uskoplje or Gornji Vakuf. In my period, until the Split agreement between Izetbegovic and Tudjman was signed, not a single Croat soldier came to this territory. As for this particular case, when I said yesterday that we had seven soldiers who were in the HV and who came after the outbreak of the war to join us, two of them were dead. This is confirmed by this document as well. I claim, with responsibility, that this document was given only so that his parents could get a retirement pension in the Republic of Croatia. It is undeniable that this late person was a member of the 4th Brigade of the Croatia army. But here this is a case of individual persons only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, it's 11.00 now. How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have much more. What I must do, and I'm cutting out stuff, but apart from a couple of more particular exhibits, I shall seek the witness's comments on a couple of the contemporaneous milinfosums so that we may have his view on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you accept --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you accept that in 1993 documents will exist, and I'm going to number them and summarise them: 385, going to the 4th Brigade of the HV army, reporting on a combatant who took part in fighting; 2407.1, an order by Andric listing five members of the 101st HV Brigade who were serving on the southern front. Do you accept that such documents would have existed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see them to tell you, otherwise I don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept -- this is 619 -- that there would be an order for all HV officers present to be listed at some stage? Do you accept that would have happened?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I've said that. That's 619. I'm not going to show it to the witness. It's just for identification at this stage. Can he see 644, please, which is similar but a different date. And simply for the Court's benefit, while that document's coming, the other documents that cover this topic are 2418, 2415, 2420, 2427.1, 2431.1, and I think 2435.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll just look at this document, Brigadier, 644. It's dated the 12th of April, 1993, it comes from Siljeg, and it's for the attention of all brigades. And it says: "Submit a list of all HV officers present in your units and headquarters." It asks for the name, the father's names. "Submit the orders which authorised his referral to the HVO, rank and number of decree of promotion, the duty he's carrying out in your army, and the duties he has carried out, and submit that information to the headquarters by the 16th of April." Now, what do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to say the following: It is quite true that this order refers to the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf, that is, Uskoplje, but it is also quite true that there were no such officers, that is, HV officers in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say, then, as an officer that had been in central headquarters, what do you say to the fact that this order was submitted to all these areas? It shows, doesn't it, as clear as daylight that there was a substantial contribution from the HV to the fighting that was going on in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said that from every municipality, when the aggression against the Republic of Croatia began by the former Yugo army and Serb renegades, there would be a man from here and from there going from Bosnia-Herzegovina to join the Croatian army in its defence. When the war broke out in our country, those men came back to our territories to defend them. These were in no way organised units of the Croatian army. Those were individuals who had been born in the area, so that -- that I mentioned here. In Gornji Vakuf, I already told you, we had seven such soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of that answer, if the following exhibit's in court, I will ask you to look at one more exhibit, 2415, if it's there. I think I've been given an incorrect reference, in which case -- unless I can have the document again. Can I look at what the witness has, please? Can I just have a copy of that myself? Thank you very much. Yes, I may have given an incorrect reference, and unless I can come back to it, I'll have to leave that point. Your Honour, just give me a minute. No, I'll let Ms. Verhaag do it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to ask you very briefly, please, Brigadier, about Ahmici. Are you saying you know absolutely nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Ahmici happened at the time when I had already left the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in regular contact with headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the main one. With the command of the Operative Zone Tomislavgrad, where I belonged at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Court that you had no knowledge of any preparations of the deployment of troops in the middle of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you saying that in all the period of time that has passed since then, neither Blaskic, nor Kordic, nor anyone else has ever explained to you what happened in Ahmici; are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've met Blaskic since then, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was in August '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By that time, the massacre at Ahmici was a well-known international event and, indeed, disaster, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard from media that a crime had happened there. But who committed it and things that came to pass there, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're really saying that you never took the opportunity to ask anyone who could know and who could have told you what had happened; is that your case, is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. And, Your Honours, if I may, I really never discussed that crime with anyone, because I simply had too many problems of my own and other things I had to do in order to tire myself with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on to August of 1993, you've described what you say was the large-scale attack and so on. Before we look very briefly at what contemporary documents show of that, the position so far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned is that it was always capable of being reinforced from Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What forces do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you, the HVO, always in a position to draw on the road from Mostar for reinforcements if you required them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road to Mostar could not be used because of military operations in Jablanica and below it, and it was only the bottleneck that we used was the Vran Mountain and we had connection with Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were able to draw on reinforcements when you required them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That meant that in real terms in Gornji Vakuf, the HVO were always in the position to call the shots, to set the agenda, however you describe it, ultimately. The HVO were always in charge, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, which was defending positions in Gornji Vakuf, that is, Uskoplje, did not have anything more than the Muslim side or, rather, the BH army. The BH army had connections with Bugojno, Novi Travnik and Travnik. And our Operative Zone, the one that we belonged to, was Tomislavgrad, and it was made of the municipalities as listed in earlier documents that you showed to me. And we were using only and exclusively the mountain -- the forest road across Vran in order to reach the civilised world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You describe an incident concerning a humanitarian convoy which you say was subject of advice by priests Milicevic and Tomas. Can you give me any information that will enable me to date that event? Is there any document you can point to that will tell me a little more detail about it? If you can't, I'm not in a position to deal with it at all.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that in mid-June, and I really wouldn't know the exact date, a humanitarian convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... your evidence. I simply want to know can you point me to a date, a document, or something that it going to enable me to deal with this in detail? Because otherwise, I simply can't.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honours, I do not have any document in my possession. If there is such a document, then it must be somewhere in the archives. But I do not have any document with me that would deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't cross-examine on that topic. Likewise, the incident you've spoken of involving the old man and his daughter, Okadar, it's not something which I'm in a position to deal with one way or the other. The Ante Starcevic Brigade was named after a person who was what?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very prominent political figure in the Croat history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What period of the Croat history?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With which political group was he associated, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man who tried to create a homeland for Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he, in short, a member of the Ustasha and a prominent one?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he associated with that group?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think there's any way in which using his name, in an area where there were other ethnicities apart from the Croats, was a provocative act?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not, because the name of Ante Starcevic was mentioned a great deal before the World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake about the original exhibit I was asking you about, the contribution of the HV. Can he see 2420, please, which is the exhibit I should have asked him to look at, and very briefly. This comes from Gornji Vakuf, from your brigade, from Zrinko Tokic. It's dated the 16th of May, and it goes to the 2nd Brigade of the Croatian army. It requests that they leave their officer, Mate Kunkic, at the disposal of the brigade in the zone of the brigade's responsibility. It goes on in the second paragraph to say: "Given that we are familiar with your plan to withdraw Officer Mate Kunkic from this area soon, we ask you not to do so until further notice," and it sets out reasons. And without going into those reasons in detail, Brigadier, if you go down two paragraphs, you'll see it says this: "In all battles so far, each person had their individual place and role, but Mr. Mate Kunkic has traced a special place for himself," and so on. This document is the clearest possible evidence of contribution from active HV units of important personnel to your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. I knew personally late Mate Kunkic. He was born in a village next to me, the village of Paloc, municipality of Gornji Vakuf, and that is where he lived until the outbreak of war in Croatia. He studied there, and he reported to the Croatian army. When the war broke out, late Mate Kunkic came to his own turf because his parents, his family, his wife and his children lived there. It is also correct that late Mate Kunkic had a say -- had a certain influence in one of the units within Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, that is, the reconnaissance company which was made up exclusively of students -- of young lads, of students who all knew one another and who all belonged to one and the same generation of people. And that means that Mate Kunkic here is an individual and in no way an organised unit of the Croatian army active in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you would accept from the document that we've looked at, that to retain him you had to seek permission from the HV, who had apparently deployed him there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did not say that those men were not members of the Croatian army, and he was a member of the Croatian army. But with the outbreak of the war in our lands, all those men who were there, and it is -- they are seven, they total seven -- they came and reported to the staff in Uskoplje, that is, Gornji Vakuf, and spent there a certain period of time. It is correct that Mate Kunkic sought this certificate presumably to justify his absence from his mother republic, that is, in the Croatian army. But one cannot say that the Croatian army operated there, because it was not an organised unit; it was an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally on this general topic, do you know a soldier or did you know a soldier called Ivica Jeger?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any newspaper articles published by any soldiers, whether by this man or not, explaining how they were -- in 1993 -- explaining how they were finding themselves fighting in your area, coming, as they did, from Croatia? Did you see any such newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't know those articles, I don't know who wrote them, but as of May, or rather early June 1993, until I was wounded, there was neither a shop there, a news shop, or any newspapers, because there was only fierce fighting. And I was then wounded and went to hospital and I returned in 1994, and I really know nothing about any article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you accept --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you accept that on the 26th of May of 1993, you will have been the officer to organise the oath-taking ceremony for new recruits? I've got the document if you want to have a look at it, but will you accept that from me?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you explain to the Judges why, in your own itinerary of events to happen at the oath-taking, the music to be played included the national anthem of Croatia, when your interest, as you tell us, was in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why play the national anthem of Croatia for such new recruits, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had no other anthem, and we are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it occur to you that playing the Croatian national anthem might itself be provocative to others in the same way as -- did it occur to you that might be provocative?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm answering loudly and clearly that there were no other peoples there as of the January conflict. The municipality and people were divided; on one side there were Croats, and on the other, Muslims. So we could not really offend anyone with it. And that was the will of the Croat people in those lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not play a piece of music, or the national anthem, associated with the very republic in whose interest you say you were fighting, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any such music, so we did not air that. We aired the Croatian anthem. And that was not the only such instance. People often requested and listened to that anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You knew, as did many members of the HVO, that one of the aims of all your efforts was possible unification of a part of the territory with Croatia, didn't you? You knew that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true. The only purpose of the unit I belonged to, Dr. Ante Starcevic, was to preserve the Croats against the persecution of the Muslim invasion, as of January 1993, until the signing of Dayton Accords. No annexation, no integration with the Republic of Croatia. I never said anything like that to my soldiers or to my subordinates, because I simply never believed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll now deal with what you say happened in August of 1993. You say there was a large-scale attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can he have, please, Exhibit 1154.1. Coming up. Now, this document, Your Honour, is dated the 4th of July of 1993, but it seems to -- it may well be that the date is incorrect, because the milinfosum is numbered and the adjacent numbers all relate to August of 1993, and that would fit in with the date given by the witness yesterday as the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is an English document, and I can tell you, Brigadier, that it's dated the 4th of July but that there may be reason to doubt the accuracy of the date. It probably should be the 4th of August. And in respect of Gornji Vakuf, at the foot of the first page, it speaks of the following: "An intense firefight broke out in the following areas: Muslim Gornji Vakuf and the Partisan cemetery, Batusa and Trnovace, and Bistrica, Krupa, and Trnovace. During the engagements, rounds passed close to B Company's location ..." That's the British battalion. "The action was assessed as being a BiH attempt to clear the Partisan cemetery. The assault was unsuccessful, as the HVO are still present in both locations." Do you accept that that is accurate?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll pass over 6, unless anybody wants me to read it out, and go to 7. It says this: "The morning was described as relatively quiet, although a round entered the sergeant's mess accommodation ..." That's in the British battalion headquarters. "... narrowly missing one individual. At 04/1200 the HVO began firing from ..." And then there's a location given. "... into BiH-held areas, such as Relay Hill and Krupa." Do you accept that that is accurate?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are right, Mr. Prosecutor. This is a document from the month of July 1993. That's when the Muslims tried, tried, to take Krupa, Ponir and Zvizda, and they did not succeed in that. With their gunfire, as they were attacking these villages, it is true that they could have jeopardised the UN base, and these villages were in front of the UN base. The villages were attacked from the direction of the Vranica Mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you lose any heavy weaponry on that July incident, as you say it was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. In the month of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You might remember if you lost something significant, mightn't you? Because in August you did lose something significant, namely, the tank in which you were when you were injured; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because under paragraph 7, the report goes on to say this: "The tank fired between 90 and 100 rounds into those areas but was blown up itself." Was that your tank that was blown up, one that had been attacking Relay Hill and other places?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dates are confused here. This is the 4th of August. When I was injured, that is when the tank was hit by an anti-armour projectile. And the very idea of having hundreds of shells being fired, I shall take the liberty of saying that we never had that many shells for a tank. Even when we had some, we had five to eight at the most, and this tank was out of order most of the time rather than operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to complete what they say in the comment, they go on to say that a major firefight began throughout Gornji Vakuf and was still ongoing. Artillery mortars were reported as falling at the rate of approximately 4 rounds per minute. And the comment of the officers is: "The fighting is reported as being the most intense since the initial BiH attacks on the 1st of August, but is believed to be an HVO counterattack. Details are scant, it's limited at present, because Gornji Vakuf are all involved in closure of Route Diamond. It's possibly linked to this if the HVO are actually attacking. The fight for the town shows few signs of abatement and looks set to continue for some time. In both Travnik and Bugojno, the BiH had secured virtual full control by this stage." What I want to suggest to you is that when you suffered in the very bad way that you did, you were engaged in an attack by the HVO, or a counterattack, as this report suggests, if the date is indeed August.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I assert the Croatian Defence Council never carried out any attack, because we did not have the strength to do that or the equipment to do that. The command post of my brigade was in Jacija [phoen], in Gornji Vakuf, and this command post is only divided by a wire fence from the UN base. That is to say that everything that was fired at this command post and the UN base could only have been done by the other side, because it seems outrageous to me that I would be firing at my own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document to look at, which is unequivocally dated the 5th of August, is 1155.1, so it's either the following day or a month and a day or so later. And it's another milinfosum, Brigadier. That's a document from the British battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to be numbered the next in sequence. The last one was 97. This is 98. And of course the first one referred to an instance on the 1st of August. So it looks as though it was the 1st of August -- the 4th of August, rather than the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, here, Brigadier, we've got -- again, I'm sorry it's not in your own language. I'll read the passages in context, and I hope slowly enough for you to take them in. But under Gornji Vakuf there's quite a long entry, which I'll try and summarise fairly. It speaks of the heavy fighting in Gornji Vakuf, it speaks of the area around the former HVO hospital being in frames, as an example, to jog your memory. And then it says at the bottom of what is the first page: "The day before, the officer commanding B Company met with Enver Zejnilagic, commander of the 317th Brigade, who claimed the HVO initiated the action, which was an attempt to interrupt BiH communications to Novi Travnik and Travnik by severing them at Krupa. This attempt was unsuccessful." Do you accept that or do you reject that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with this report, because on the 4th of August, 1993, I was heavily wounded and I was in a coma for 11 days after that. But I know what I left behind. I know what kind of misery was left behind me. So I cannot accept this report. I know what was there, I know what I suffered. Had we attacked such a strong force, which was reinforced by the Bugojno forces and which was already in BiH army control, and part of the Mujahedin forces that were indeed strong and notorious in that area. And in the village of Voljevac and these other hamlets that are near the forest, then the 17th Krajiska Brigade. So I already mentioned, Your Honours, that I saw with my very own eyes a report that was shown to me in December, but this is not the report that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I quote what was said in this report that I saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. If Defence counsel wants to ask you something, they can in re-examination, but meanwhile, just deal with the questions which counsel asks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
