utterances.text: The British officer's report goes on to say that the only route for direct reinforcement open to the BiH is Route Diamond, which is one of their names for a route. And in reporting what they've been told by the BiH, the officer said that the BiH officer had received orders to cease offensive actions which they were obeying, and claimed to the BiH officer that his diversionary force had destroyed two T55s on the Podovi feature and also a transporter. He then goes on to say that Slobodan Praljak admitted that the reason that Route Diamond had been closed by the HVO at the Makljen checkpoint was to prevent aide convoys driving into the middle of the attack. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that, because these are fabrications of the commander of the 317th Brigade of the Muslim army who had a conversation with the commander of the U.N. unit, and what this man told him, this gentleman then wrote in his report. I know the real truth about this. Never did we have two tanks in the area, we only had one tank, and you cannot destroy two if we only had one. That is the first thing I want to say. The second thing I want to say: We did not have any kind of armoured vehicle, an ACV or anything like that. There was no transport during those days, I repeat again, until the 4th of August from Makljen onwards, and I don't think there were any convoys in the area on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case the last point I want you to deal with, Witness, is the comment of the officer. I jump over the next few lines, unless anybody wants me to read them, and the comment is this: "The situation in the town is currently a stalemate, with the BiH clearly having lost the initiative they enjoyed on the 2nd of August. The HVO have surrendered no additional ground but have been unable to rest control of former Croat areas. The fighting is currently five days' old. At a similar point in the fighting for Travnik, Kakanj and Bugojno, the BiH had all but seized the towns. The reasons for the relative BiH failure this time round are myriad but intrinsically seem to turn upon the HVO's ability and willingness to reinforce the area and their own apparent inability to do so." I suggest that the last line relates back to the BiH. But it's right, isn't it, that so far as your area is concerned, the HVO did have an ability and a willingness to reinforce the area and, by the time that you were telling the Court you suffered the very serious injury that you did, had already turned the tables on the BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH army or, rather, the Muslim army got wings, so to speak, when the towns were taken. What is stated here is not exactly correct. Until the 25th, approximately, of July 1993, Travnik, Bugojno and Kakanj were taken. They had full control under the territory over the municipality of Bugojno, the Muslim army did. They expelled 18.000 Croats and they continued their penetration towards Mostar, and they were stopped then in the area of Uskoplje. That's where the heaviest fighting was taking place. We were losing territory, Paloc, Polurici [phoen]. These are purely Croat villages traditionally, and that is where we stopped all this metal that the Muslim army had. I also wish to say that at Mount Vranica, they controlled the road to Travnik. It is not true that that is the only route. They called it Diamond. There is another one --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is going too fast for the interpreters. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down a bit for the interpreters. Yes. I think, in any event, we've dealt with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And my last questions relate to this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, in giving your evidence yesterday, and I make no complaint of this, read from the first line of paragraph 19 of your summary -- there's no need to turn to it again -- and saying the strategic goal of the Muslim leadership was to expel -- there's no need to turn to it, Brigadier -- was to expel the Croats from Central Bosnia, and you referred to some evidence in support of that. Tell us again, what is it that enables you to say that the objective of the Muslim leadership, the strategic goal, was to expel the Croats from Central Bosnia? Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I already mentioned that when I talked to my former colleagues from the former Yugoslavia, they told me that they received such and such orders, et cetera, et cetera. I don't have to repeat all of this. However, one thing is obvious, that the army, the forces of the BH army, as they attained this objective, they expel the Croats of Konjic, where the military industry is, Novi Travnik and Bugojno as well. Is this not a well-conceived policy in order to have a well-rounded process of production? And come on, you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know what your evidence is, and I think you've confirmed that your evidence comes from the contact with the two named people you've spoken of. Is that the only evidence that you're turning to to support your suggestion that this was the objective?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, then, please tell us where and when it was that you claim to have met these two men.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mid-April 1994 when, by sheer coincidence, the war operations, the combat operations, had stopped, the Washington Accords had been signed, checkpoints were established, the soldiers returned home, although there were very little homes on our side to return to because everything was devastated. And in a place called Fontana at the line of delineation -- I still used crutches because I could not walk yet -- I saw these former colleagues of mine on the other side of the street, and they were friends of mine too. And then we discussed all of this, what do we need all of this for, why was such a pretty town destroyed, why did so many people come to hate each other, such deep wounds would last for a long time. They said, "Those are the orders that we got from the military and political leadership of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," or, rather, from their superiors in Zenica, "to cleanse the territory of Central Bosnia." He did not say "Central Bosnia", he said, "cleanse the area of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, where Muslims would come to live, those that were expelled by the Bosnian Serb army." They did not attain this strategic objective of theirs. The Croats of Uskoplje remained where they had lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now I only want to know what they said. Is there anything else they said that you want to tell us about, because I want to be quite sure that we've got it accurately so that we can take the matter further. Is there anything else they said? Anything else you asked them and that they replied, please?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation -- well, let's put it this way: Let's say we sort of said hello to one another, but we gave each other dirty looks, sort of, and we kind of said hello, "Hello." The first thing I asked them was how were their families, whether they had all survived, et cetera, and then in this conversation, this chatting that went on for five or ten minutes -- no, not even five minutes -- we just talked in haste, because even a year later the Muslims were afraid to talk to us, they were afraid of their superiors. So I asked him, and he answered me the way I already explained, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, which one do you say of the two men used the word "cleansing" and said that they were given instructions by their superiors to cleanse an area, please; which one?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Fahrudin Agic, who was later trained in Pakistan after the Washington Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when he said this, it was together with the other man, was it, Goran Cisic, so that he could hear?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cisic, Cisic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they say which of their superiors had given them this extraordinary instruction?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they mentioned no names. But that's what they said, that they received orders from the political and military leadership, probably through their own chain of command, that they had to cleanse Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf and that that is where allegedly the Muslims would come to live, those who were expelled by the Bosnian Serb army from other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you write this down or report this important event at the time to anyone?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to write it down because I had a witness. Well, I'm not going to say "500 per cent", but 100 per cent invalid and a friend of mine, Borislav Posavac, who is here with me and who will confirm all of this, if necessary, this statement of mine, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you didn't record it anywhere, nowhere, did you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, had I known that this would happen, I would have recorded this on a tape-recorder. But I did not know that this would happen and that this would be needed, just like many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find yourself working with the man Fahrudin Agic at a later stage in some organisation in the area of is it Kupres?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only encountered him once in conversation with General Alagic. We were then undergoing liberation operations, we were some kind of partners then, and I saw him at the Kalin Hotel in Bugojno, and I've never met him since, I've never met him since. This could have been the end of 1994 or the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the man Cisic is now dead?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about that, I think, two or three months after he got killed. He got killed somewhere near Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm in a position to cross-examine on this material to this extent: that I must suggest to you that there was no such meeting of the type you described, and there was certainly no such acknowledgement of an instruction to cleanse an area you suggested, and that what you're telling us about that is wholly false.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that I would speak the truth. And what would give me the right now to lie and to besmirch the name of a person who is not here? It is embarrassing for me to say bad things about a person who is not present, and I never did such a thing. You asked me about this, and I responsibly state that what I said is true. I also responsibly state that I was at one of the meetings with the representatives of the BH army in Bugojno at the Hotel Kalin at the end of 1994, the beginning of 1995, in relation to the area of Kupres, or a plateau above it, as to how far a unit should go. This was at General Alagic's, and that's when I saw Agic again. I gave him a cigarette and we smoked a cigarette together at the door of this hotel, and that is how we talked. I have to mention, if I already haven't said this, this Fahrudin Agic is four years younger than I am. We were together for about ten years. We grew up in the same village. His house and my house are about 150 metres away from each other. So we knew each other very well. That is why I want to say that this is what a man I know very well told me and who was a high officer in the BH army, and also he was my boss in the former army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I propose to ask on that. As the Court will understand, I can't deal with it in great detail. But as to the specific allegations put, that's challenged, and I will return to it at a later stage in the trial, if necessary. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Sekerija, a few final questions. Let us just conclude this subject. These two gentlemen or, rather, Mr. Agic, you said, if you agree with me, that you heard certain pieces of information from imprisoned BH army soldiers who were not from the area of Uskoplje or Gornji Vakuf but also from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honours, in conversations with persons who had stayed behind, who were imprisoned or who did not get out on time, usually one would take prisoner persons who were members of the 317th Brigade or, rather, who were in the BH army. I didn't know their chain of command, nor was I particularly interested in it. However, when we talked to these men, when we asked them where they were from, for example, the person would say that he's from Jajic [phoen] or somewhere in Eastern Bosnia, and I personally asked one such man who had been taken prisoner -- I personally asked him, I said, "Man, what are you looking for in this area?" The official leadership of their army, the military and the political leadership, he said, "promised us that we could come to live in any Croat village that we took." That is the truth. Could I just say one more thing? Could I just add one more thing? I would like to corroborate this by saying the following: I think there is some kind of written trace of this in the archives of this former unit of mine or whatever. I think there is a written trace with the chief of security or somebody who was carrying out these interrogations. This is not a fabrication, and I do not want to deceive the Court and I do not wish to lie here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. I believe this matter is clear. I have quite a number of questions about documents, because so many of them were shown to you, but let us try to do it very briefly and clearly and try to finish as quickly as possible. 298.3 mentions the Ustasha flag. I do not really want to tax the patience of the Honourable Court with this, but you're telling us that you always and invariably referred to the flag of the Croat people; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you used a phrase and you said it was never a Ustasha flag, and you gave us the colours of that flag. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it vexed the Muslim side, the flag that was hoisted up on the post office on the eve of the Christmas, then this was the flag of the Croat people, the Croat flag, the tricolour red/white/blue with the Croat coat of arms in the middle, and that was the flag that was there and it was no Ustasha flag, because the Ustasha flag is very different from the Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Just one last question about that. Did you ever hoist up a black banner, a black flag, or whatever Ustasha used as their emblems in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Z298.5, it is about those villages there, and Zenica, and things like that. You answered a moment ago that you had no artillery pieces to fire on those villages because they were too far away from the town; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So if there were any combat operations in that area, it had nothing to do with the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because our artillery, if you look at the map, I can show you the positions where the mortars were and what was their ultimate range. It's about 3.800 metres to 4.200, and not even in theory could we reach the area that was covered by the Muslims. So perhaps there could have been some individual operations between Prozor and Rama and the Muslim army on the other side which was bordering on that side with Uskoplje, that is, Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We have to wait a little bit because of interpretation. Let us move on to Z372.2. That was a report written, as it says -- or rather signed by the commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic, and at the bottom we also have the name of Dzemal Merdan, so it is a document which was written for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecutor insisted on the word "ultimatum" or, rather, that you, the Croats, had issued the BH army with an ultimatum. However, I must say that here this document, that is, the paragraph one before last -- no, the second before last on the third page, that it was a categorical stance, not the ultimatum; that is how it is interpreted. But I want to ask you once again. Even though you took no part in those negotiations, did you, the Croats, mean the brigade Dr. Ante Starcevic that you were a part of, and did you issue the advisory with any kind of ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such documents with the signature of Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Dzemal Merdan were, rather than mentioned, they are just the scum of the earth, they are the warmongers of the Muslim people, they are the riffraff. And a lot of this has been mentioned, but you find it only document [as interpreted] that they write to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Z236.18, and that is an order by General Bobetko of May '92?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So my basic question is: This document of May 5th, '92, who was your enemy in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, who was the common enemy of the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, the army of Bosnian Serbs, supported by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move on. Chronologically speaking, this question comes as the logical second question. It was said a great deal about Mr. Kordic, who was advocating to split the weapons, to divide the weapons on a 50/50 basis, and the Prosecutor said that that is something that the Ministry of Defence normally would be dealing with. So my question is: Do you know at all when the Department of Defence of the Croat Defence Council was founded?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in '93/'94, because nothing worked, really. I told you it was the armed people. No army from barracks had ever come out. It was the people who armed themselves. Some bought rifles. They took the money out of their own pockets to purchase some weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you spoke about the distribution of weapons, at that time the JNA still had its barracks in the area -- if you are not really well, shall we --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. I shall try to do it faster. So I was about to ask: The time that we are talking about, May '92, would you agree with me that the JNA at that time still held the barracks in early May '92 both in Travnik, and the depot at Slimena, and Kiseljak, Kaonik, and who knows where else?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you, the Croats, and also the TO, that is, the Muslims at that time were operating on a sort of semi-legal basis, because the JNA was still in that area?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So these are the early days of the organisation, both yours and the TO's?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. And those are -- now the letter, 207. This was also discussed a great deal. I don't have it here. But be that as it may, it's a letter. It is a handwritten letter, and you commented on it when it was shown you by the Prosecution. The period of time referred to in the document, that is, fighting in Jajce, going to Jajce, and so on and so forth, it is fighting against whom?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighting against Serbs, because it is Serbs all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this document that you were given, you told us that was not an order; it was just an information or something like that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a request, no order. Please, please, get us three vehicles and transfer this humanitarian relief. It must have contained flour, perhaps some tins, perhaps some fuel, to supply the hospital in Jajce, which was simply full to the brim with the wounded. I don't have anything of any military order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Z248 was another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sekerija, are you all right? Would you like a break?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll somehow manage to the end. At times my hands begin to -- I get a tremor in my hands. But it takes only three to five minutes, and no longer. No problem. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Naumovski, perhaps you can be as rapid as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes, perhaps. I'll do my best. I'll hurry things up. Yes, why don't you have some water. I was about to suggest it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is not the first time it happens to me. So what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So 248. You said that you forwarded the information that you received, that is, General Petkovic's order. But in this document it is curious that the addressees are to the towns Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that agrees with what you explained. This document, the 23rd of October, 1992, this is your signature. I am not a handwriting expert, but I think it is different from your other signatures. But you mentioned that you were in a cast, in a plaster cast at that time, so could you please explain to us how could you sign it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time -- well, you can see it. I still have some screws in this hand and I also have some rods in my shoulder. So at that time I was still wearing a plaster cast. So if you compare my signature now and my signature then, they look alike, but they're not identical. Because at that time, I was telling you, I was still on a sick leave and I was still in a plaster cast, but I went back to the headquarters of my brigade and I did as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: 261 is a document, and His Honour Judge Bennouna had questions to ask you about it. Have you ever heard, to begin with, something were to be deputy commander of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna? Have you heard --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is the deputy commander of a military unit or a vice-president of the political leadership, a vice-president of, but a deputy commander can exist only in a military unit. But there is no such thing as the deputy commander of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. I think it was a mistake, somebody slipped or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And when asked by the Prosecutor and by His Honour Judge Bennouna, you gave us your view about this document. But I'm not quite sure whether you really got the gist of what His Honour was asking you, so that I shall repeat the question. We can show you this document if you wish, but perhaps you already know what document we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will this document please be shown, Z261. Will the usher please help the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will Mr. Naumovski please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you this question now. His Honour asked you, but I'm not sure that you understood what he was driving at. Does this document show that Mr. Kordic was part of the chain of command, military chain of command, or not? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Do you want to read it or --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any country, and in any war, the military hierarchy was accounted to the political leadership of a country, of a region, or a municipality. So what we are dealing with here, this is not a document of military nature, the deployment or use of forces, taking positions, defensive positions. That is out of the question. The only thing it can be to, that the bravest, the most loyal sons of the Croat people are being sent to where they should be sent in order to rescue those famished, starving, emaciated people of Jajce, and with that I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And yet another question about this document. According to you, does this document mean an invitation to defend it at all costs, or is it a surrender of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are cries for help. These are wails for help rather than invitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Document 2404.1, that is, the letter about the death of late Stanko Posavac. Just one detail which nobody pointed out, and you must know it, because Posavac is a surname from your area. Posavac, son of Branjo, is from Gornji Vakuf. He was born there, isn't it, and he was buried there too?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is the irony of the whole thing, because his mother and my mother are two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So he was your nephew?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us move on. There is a handout by Siljeg, Z644, addressed to all the brigades. Evidently it is a routine letter seeking information about those HV members.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I have already said, and I shall never go back on that: It is quite true that in our area, or rather from our area, from Uskoplje/Gornji Vakuf, in the beginning of the war in 1991, some Croats left and went to fight with the Croatian army. And when the war broke out in our lands, those men came back. It is seven individuals that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, my last question about this: You do not know whether those men had regulated the status with the HV or not?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was mention -- there were several questions about Ante Starcevic. I do not know whether this witness knows or not, but it is for the sake of the Court that I will say this, even though it is not the subject. Ante Starcevic is a well-known Croatian intellectual thinker, politician, who was active in late 19th century in Austria Hungary at that time and who was upholding and fighting for the rights of Croats. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to give evidence, you better go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If it were a fact or something, I wouldn't have, but I think this was simply a question to do with history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There was also mention about the Croatian anthem in the area of Uskoplje in May 1993. Which anthem did the Croats play after the war, that is, after the Washington Accords were signed in 1994, 1995, in Uskoplje and in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats invariably played the Croatian anthem, not only before that, but 1994, 1995, until an anthem was written for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But the anthem that is played now, that anthem was prescribed --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The higher representative, the higher representative, because three peoples could not agree on one common anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So every people had his own?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they use them to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is the end of my re-examination, and I should like to thank Mr. Sekerija for his patience, especially during these last five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I've been through worse things before. This was quite all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier Sekerija, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released, free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Drmic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, as you can see, the next four witnesses are produced to talk about two separate sets of issues. In that regard, Mr. Drmic and Mr. Vinac basically talk about the same incident. And we've submitted to the Court, or actually we filed before they testified, the affidavits of two other corroborative witnesses, Ivica Drmic and Franjo Drmic. The next two witnesses deal with the Kacuni checkpoint incident, that is, Mr. Grubesic and Mr. Arar, and we have filed, prior to their testimony, three corroborative affidavits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we've seen those yet, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have extra copies, if the Court wishes. We actually filed them this morning. Those are of Mr. Milenko Arapovic, Mr. Brano Kristo, and Mr. Bogdan. They're all extremely short and they deal with specific facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be sensible to take the break now, I think, rather than start the witness, and we'll come back at 20 past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we should get through these four witnesses fairly rapidly, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I certainly hope so. We may -- I want to alert the Court, if we get through these witnesses as rapidly as I certainly hope we will, we may run out of evidence this week. We have only one more witness who's scheduled to come in this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we understand the difficulties of getting witnesses in the particular circumstances of this Tribunal, so for the moment there would be no criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for an hour and a half. Twenty past 2.00, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're just waiting for our next witness, Mr. Branko Drmic, to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I believe your name is Branko Drmic, and you were born on August the 22nd, 1955, in the town of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few very preliminary matters, Mr. Drmic. You are a Bosnian Croat, and a Roman Catholic by religion, a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are married, sir, and you have two children, and you currently live with your family in the town of Vitez today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you received your primary and secondary education in Vitez, and then you completed two years of high school in Sarajevo, graduating from the High School for Social Work in 1978?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And before the civil war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you worked at the Vitez Slobodan Princip Seljo factory in that town, in the purchasing and marketing division of the business; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you own a bar in the village of Donja Veceriska called the Cafe Ravne?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I, Branko Drmic, together with my brother, Franjo Drmic, had a cafe together with my brother in Ravne. It was called Cafe Ravne.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this cafe, sir, was located actually in your brother's house in Donja Veceriska, even though you owned it, the cafe, that is, I believe.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. A compromise solution was found. The house was his, and the cafe was owned by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you both ran it together --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: It was in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry. And you ran it together with your brother, Franjo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, is it fair to say that Donja Veceriska is a very small village and that it had only a total population of about 700 before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that Donja Veceriska had a population of about 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, we have made you aware that a man by the name of Midhat Haskic has made a statement which has been admitted into evidence in this case. In that statement, he claims that Mr. Dario Kordic was supposedly in the Cafe Ravne, your bar, for several hours during the evening of April the 15th, 1993, and that he was attending a party for Mile Vinac's son. Could you tell us, is that contention true or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that contention is not true, because on that day and at that time, Dario Kordic did not come to the Cafe Ravne. The village is a very small one. On that day, I worked after 5.00 p.m. That is to say, on that day, Dario Kordic was not in this cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you have recognised Mr. Kordic if he had been in the cafe, sir, and if so, could you tell the Court precisely how?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I certainly would have recognised Mr. Dario Kordic, first of all, because he was a well-known figure. That is to say, I knew him through the media. He has a very special kind of hair style. His hair is cut in a special way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Has Mr. Kordic ever visited your bar at any time or during the time that you owned it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: No, no. To the best of my knowledge, Dario Kordic was never in Donja Veceriska, and he absolutely never visited the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Two more minor matters. Can you tell us, Mr. Drmic, was Mr. Mile Vinac in your cafe on the evening of April the 15th, 1993, as contended by Mr. Haskic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mile Vinac was not in the Cafe Ravne on that day either. Midhat Haskic was not in the cafe on that day either. So that statement is incorrect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second matter of detail, Mr. Drmic. Could you tell us whether, as far as you know, Mr. Kordic has ever been to Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat. As far as I know, Dario Kordic was never in the village of Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell the Judges, please, a little bit about Midhat Haskic? Do you know him? If so, what do you know about him, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Midhat Haskic very well. He is a man who, in his 30s and 40s, was involved in business. He had asthma, that is to say that he had lung problems. Although he was not allowed to drink, he would have a drink every now and then. When he would have a drink too many, he would be known to provoke other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any view on whether he was a man who could be trusted? Could you give your views to the Trial Chamber on that particular subject, sir, or don't you have a view on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: If the honourable Trial Chamber wishes to hear my opinion, I believe that this person cannot be trusted 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say he was not in your bar on the 15th of April, 1993. How can you be sure of that, Mr. Drmic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I am sure because of the events that followed. I kept thinking about this for a long time, what had been happening in general at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you remember an incident in which the house and the bar were damaged before, in the month before the time when Mr. Kordic is alleged to have visited your bar, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I remember that incident. That incident occurred about a month before the conflict broke out. I think it was during the night. We cannot exactly ascertain at what time this happened. A few explosive devices were thrown at the cafe. One exploded in the parking lot in front of the cafe. That is to say that when we look at the entrance of the cafe, the right-hand side was -- the right-hand glass was broken, and a bullet went through this glass and ended in the bar itself, and I think that there are marks from this shrapnel until the present day. On the next day we found two more unexploded explosive devices. Perhaps I should be more specific. We saw that these two explosive devices were made of cans, of tins.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you. If the Prosecution has any questions about those matters of detail, then you can certainly elaborate upon that, but let's just go on, because I have just two more questions for you. Did Muslims continue coming to your bar, Muslim people from Donja Veceriska, or elsewhere, after the bomb incident in March of 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Until this incident, they came to our bar regularly. However, after this incident, spontaneously, no one entered our bar. I believe that a considerable part of the Muslim population was simply ashamed of entering our cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did that include Mr. Midhat Haskic, or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the conflict, who was in the majority in Donja Veceriska, Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, the number was equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or may it be the case that there was even a Muslim majority there before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there was any deviation, I was not aware of these figures. However, this possibility does exist, because quite a few refugees moved into Donja Veceriska over a very short period of time. I'm referring to Muslim refugees, that is to say, the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And immediately after the conflict, how many Muslims were there in Donja Veceriska? None?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can you cite any Muslims who were living there immediately after the conflict, just so that I can check it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to complete the picture of the ethnic composition and ethnic affections and disaffections in the village, first the topography of the place. It's a kilometre or so outside of Vitez on ground that rises up from a plain; would that be about correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can give my version of where the village of Donja Veceriska is. That is to say that Donja Veceriska is on a small hill about 4 kilometres away from Vitez. That is to say that a part of the village of Donja Veceriska borders on the business compound of Vitezit. And it is precisely this part, Your Honours, that borders on Vitezit, has a Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's an isolated but visible community; that is to say, it's separate, but you can see it from the road, and you can see the main road from it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This statement is correct. I do not understand what you consider to be the main road, because if you look from Jardol, you can see all of Donja Veceriska. And naturally, it's the other way around too. From the village of Donja Veceriska, you can see this road which goes around Vitez, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Its proximity to the Vitezit factory made it strategically important to the HVO; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for us, that is to say, all the villagers of the village of Donja Veceriska, the business was very important for all of us. Ninety per cent of us were employed there, and that was our only source of revenue. So from my own point of view, I'm saying that this was a very interesting business, where people earned their salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I image you understand what I mean by something being strategically important in the time of the conflict of the HVO. That's what I'm asking you about in relation to this factory. Do you accept that it was strategically important to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is not a soldier, is not being put forward as one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you a member of the HVO, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Starting when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I, Branko Drmic, was a member of the HVO from the 25th of February, 1992. That is to say, with your permission -- or I don't know if there are going to be other questions related you to this -- I was first mobilised within the defence department of the Territorial Defence in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need for the time being. Thank you. Concluding what I wanted to ask you about the composition and ethnic attitudes in general within the village, would you accept that by, say, about 1998, I think, if one of the Muslims whose house had been destroyed in the conflict wanted to return to Donja Veceriska, the atmosphere in the village was such that his house might still be burnt down before he was able to return? Would you accept that that happened as late as 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say that now, that is to say, before I came here, as concerns the village of Donja Veceriska, the complete Bosniak population has returned. I cannot make any comments about this incident. That is to say that Bosnia and Herzegovina is becoming a state where there is rule of law. There are institutions that can and should resolve all negative developments that may be taking place anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To conclude that topic, as a matter of fact, do you know the house or the location of the house of the man Nesim Haskic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that house was blown up before he was able to return to it, as recently as a couple of years ago?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we are talking about Nesib Haskic, there was an old house that belonged to his parents, and he also had a newly-built house which was only covered. During the war, and I don't know why, part of the house remained roofless. That is the only thing I know about this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you say of Midhat, who I think would be a relation of Nesim, perhaps his cousin, you say he was not to be trusted 100 per cent. Now, don't be embarrassed. Just tell us, because the Judges need to know this, why.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: During the first part, I already said that he liked to drink, and when he would have a drink too many, he would sometimes say a word or two that were superfluous, and he was not a trustworthy person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first account of this, in answer to Mr. Sayers, was, I think, that he said things that were provocative, unless my recollection is wrong. Being provocative doesn't make you, in any sense, unreliable. Is it these provocative words that you rely on to say that he's not to be trusted 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Midhat Haskic very well. He would offend a person by way of a joke, and if he was under the influence of some alcohol as well, then that was no longer the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, of course, as is obvious and has been famously said, you can be drunk in the evening, but in the morning, you're sober. When sober, he was not provocative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I have to repeat what I said. He tried to be funny, and his humour would become embarrassing at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And sober, there would be no reason not to trust his word, at least when he wasn't being funny, would there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on several occasions I already stated my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you, please, to help me and the Judges with some other things that Midhat Haskic has said. You haven't seen him, I think, for many years, and are you aware that he's dead?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you were to ask me about the year, I would not know, but I have heard that Midhat Haskic allegedly died. That is the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, in the HVO, can confirm that your cafe served the purpose not just of being a cafe but it was also a command post, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, until the conflict broke out, the cafe only worked as a cafe. However, after the conflict broke out, the defence department mobilised the entire facility; that is to say that it was mostly only used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it the only cafe in Donja Veceriska at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has it been renovated and rebuilt since?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you know what are the conditions of life in general in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The inventory is the same, and here or there, one works a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But has it been rebuilt or renovated perhaps in the last couple of years or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, nothing except that windows were glazed and that it was painted inside. Nothing was added to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a photograph of -- a recent photograph of what looks like a cafe in Donja Veceriska, and it may show the way the cafe was. But it may be it's an entirely different picture of an entirely different building, so I wanted to know what had happened. Just have a look at it very quickly. Tell me if this relates to your cafe or not, and if it doesn't, we'll take it no further.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the pictures of the cafe. However, this part that was built on, I see it as the exterior, and only the terrace had been covered. I understood the question to mean whether the interior of the cafe had been renovated, added, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Put the other photograph on the ELMO as well, please. This shows from a vehicle with a mirror on it, as you can see, driving in the direction of Vitez along the street of Donja Veceriska, the cafe on the left-hand side. Is that broadly the same size as the cafe was at the time of these events in April '93?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the cafe covered an area of some 80 metres square. At present, I, Branko Drmic, have in one part. Looking at this photograph, in the left part I have another business of my own, a shop. And my brother, Franjo Drmic, in its other part now has a cafe of his own. And this situation has existed for the past three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photographs, then, seem to be helpful. They are numbered 2820.1, and the other one is numbered 2820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to admit those?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm neutral. The Court has seen them. I only want them for the size of the building, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll let them be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This bar, and we now can see its size, you see, was well able to accommodate the local HVO, of which you were a member before this conflict, and it regularly enough did so; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that until the conflict broke out, the cafe was only a cafe. And there are also documents to show when the cafe was mobilised and demobilised. At that time it served for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In explaining to the Judges how it was you were able to say that Midhat Haskic was not in the cafe on the night in question, you said, "I've kept thinking about this." When did you first have any reason, please, to think about this particular night and about whether Midhat Haskic was there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with my family and friends, I analysed frequently the course of events, and as a man who is concentrating on business, think that the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was struck by a terrible disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But when did you first have to think back, please, as you tell us you have done, to the night of the 15th of April and to whether Mr. Midhat Haskic was in your cafe on that night, or not? When did you start that mental process?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I already said, Your Honours, that something that leaves an impression on you by itself will also leave some trace in a man, so these things are imprinted on my mind since before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my pressing you on this, but what was there about April the 15th, 1993 that made it stick out from April 14th or the 13th or the 12th? What was so important about that night that it sits in your memory, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot -- I don't know how to explain it to you. Simply, certain things seem more noteworthy, such as the ones -- we are simply compelled to remember the date of birth of your child, the date of your marriage, as well as something bad, such as a day before the break-out of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I can accept that you might have this day in mind, but that it wouldn't, on your account, I think, be important until after the event. Or was there something happening that night that made it important at the time it was happening, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I have already said it, and repeatedly so, Your Honours. I do not know how else to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me help you. In fact, the 15th probably does stick out in your memory, because that was the day, or one of the days, when the Croat population was being evacuated from your village, ahead of the conflict. Why were the civilian Croats being evacuated ahead of the conflict, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that contention is completely untrue. For instance, my family, and very many other Croat families, were not evacuated. If necessary, we can list a number of other reasons during the shelling by the Yugoslav People's Army of the industrial complex at Vitezit. On two occasions my family fled to Croatia, and then we simply got inured to those things. So that day my family was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But other Croat families had left, and they had left because they had been warned to go. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can remind you that before the conflict broke out, there were a number of adversities. One of them was the capture of Zivko Totic, and when some of his escorts were killed, all of us, all of us, did not approach this same problem, because some were more cautious than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say a family fled as far away as Croatia. Why go all the way to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, because there was a general feeling of uncertainty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in this part of Central Bosnia. You're aware that war began in one town, another town, third, fourth, and unfortunately some people who did not believe that war would break out in their town unfortunately paid it with their life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on. I just want to -- your last answer on this. Is it a correct picture of that bar of yours and of the small village of Donja Veceriska, on the night of the 15th, that a large number of Croats had moved out and that there were a large number of HVO soldiers in your bar? Is that the picture that should be painted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as on previous days, on that day, the 15th, was just a day like any other; for me, just another working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's really your case, you see, if that's really your account, if it's just another working day, we come back to the first question: Why should Midhat Haskic feature so prominently by his absence or presence? And you simply say that you can remember it, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought that you understood what I meant when I said that after the explosive devices were thrown at our outlet, nobody -- none of the Bosniaks came again to our outlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you at about 2.00 in the morning of the 16th, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was at home, asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By what were you awakened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at 2.00 I wasn't roused by anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no attack on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is way beyond the scope of the direct examination. I didn't ask him anything about that whatsoever. I asked him only about a very limited subject. That's why he was brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In this case it doesn't matter, because it goes to his credit about his evidence as to what happened a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying there was no attack at all on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this last question you asked me, in the evening of the 16th, and I was at home, asleep. And on the 16th, in the morning, I heard a couple of bursts of fire, and I thought then that once again somebody perhaps had got drunk and fired just like that. But then a number of events succeeded one another very quickly, and at 6.00, with my family, I evacuated, that is, my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a member of the HVO, you would no doubt learn, if not the same night, thereafter, what had happened. Let's deal with that in two stages. Did you learn, or indeed see, the same night what was happening metres from your house, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that night, that is, I did not notice anything that would -- that might indicate anything out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, having heard these two explosions or whatever they were, did you telephone anyone? Or come to that, did you receive phone calls from anyone?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. Neither did I make phone calls, nor did anyone notify me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no reason to believe that your phone line had been cut?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that neither did I call anyone, nor did anyone call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you've spoken to people since. There was no reason to believe the Croats' telephone lines were cut that night, was there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the telephone lines were in working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, in the same statement that Midhat Haskic deals with what he saw in your cafe, he said that he realises his phone was dead and he had to move from house to house. Any reason for the Judges to doubt the accuracy of that part of his statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He tells the reader of the statement, does the late Midhat Haskic, that he saw five soldiers in his brother's yard at about half past 2.00, one of whom was Franjo Sapina and then another man called Cano, son of Anto, together with two men from Mosunj. Any reason to doubt that, or perhaps you can confirm some of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He goes on, in the same statement, to explain how his brother was gunned down by the man -- probably by the man Franjo, or certainly by the man Franjo Sapina.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had been woken up. Were you looking out of your window or what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my house is near -- that is, near the cafe, some ten metres behind it, and the easiest way for me is to go out through the back door, so I go out into the garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I needn't trouble you with perhaps some of these details if this is the position: Is it going to be your position, please, that you saw nothing of what was happening all night and were able to evacuate your family the following morning, still totally ignorant of happenings that night, and that you remain ignorant of what happened that night to this day; is that going to be your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my position is that there was nothing out of the ordinary that night either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing out of the ordinary. What happened to the houses of the Muslims of Donja Veceriska at the time of this conflict on the 16th of April of 1993, what happened to the houses of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the morning, when I heard the gunfire and explosions, after about 15 or 20 minutes I realised that the Muslims had attacked us, and so I, number one, evacuated my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Just an attack by the Muslims, was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since you understand it was an attack by the Muslims, can you explain then, please, how it was that Midhat Haskic's brother was killed? It may even be his throat was cut.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not -- I am completely unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both at the time and since?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after a while -- and I must say that I really am sorry for all the victims of either ethnicity -- I learned that there were fatalities amongst the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us then, please, now that you've learned about it, how they came about if they didn't come about because they were attacked by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm unaware of that. I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the houses that we've been dealing with -- that would be the house of the relation of Midhat -- was actually blown up by bombs that very night. Are you really telling the Court that you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or of the shelling that happened to the village later on that night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: I can't hear. There's some interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shelling that happened to that village that night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the truth is exactly as Midhat Haskic described it in his statement, and you probably know that. And the truth was that on that night, the 15th, there was a gathering of HVO soldiers in your cafe in the way they regularly gathered there, and that's the truth you daren't explain to this Court. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the tension was rather high because of a series of incidents, it was common to see in the village both Bosniak troops and Croat troops, so that it was a common occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to the question. In your cafe, on your own account, the only soldiers you would expect to find on the 15th of April would be the HVO. Are you now accepting there were soldiers there, and if so, was it the HVO, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat that there was the usual -- the common number of patrons as was normal in the earlier days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kordic was there as well, and he was spending time with a man, Vinac, who was pleased or complimented by Kordic's intimacy with him, by his closeness to him; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said -- I have already given my answer to this question. Neither Kordic nor Mile Vinac were in my cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How about Ivica Drmic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ivica Drmic was an HVO member, and at that time he was commanding a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying, by that answer, that he was or that he was not present in your cafe, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot recall all the names and persons. If I could, I'd be a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So Ivica may have been there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DRMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you assume -- I can't give an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must suggest to you that Ivica Drmic was not only there but he was communicating regularly -- talking regularly to Kordic and, indeed, giving him pieces of paper with intelligence or information on them. As a company commander, he might have access to information, mightn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for comment. I think we've got the witness's evidence on these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. In fact, I've come to the end of what I wanted to ask in any event. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Drmic, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go, now that it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Your Honours, our next witness is Mile Vinac. I believe he will be brought in any minute now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, we'll go on until 10 past 4.00, so if you come to a convenient moment then, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I will finish the examination-in-chief even earlier. We are in your hands. However, we haven't got too much of a programme for the next two days, so I believe that we will deal with all our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, we can start with the questions. Please give us your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Mile Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, you were born on the 23rd of January, 1960, in the village of Donja Veceriska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Honourable Trial Chamber has already heard about the fact that this is a village that is relatively close to the town of Vitez. Tell us, please, you completed elementary school in Vitez and secondary school in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After completing your secondary school education, you became a mechanic?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are married, and you have four children?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you still all live together in Donja Veceriska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, like most of your other fellow villagers, you worked in the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us not confuse the Honourable Judges. That was the previous name of the factory, and later it was renamed Vitezit. But it's the same factory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: By ethnicity you are a Bosnian Croat, you are Roman Catholic by religion, and you are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please, because of the interpretation that is involved into the official languages of the Tribunal, please don't hurry too much with your answers. And as concerns your CV, you entered the military when the war broke out, and you're a professional officer until the present day?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are a captain in the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And at present, you work in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, with regard to your CV, just one more thing. You have a nickname. What was the nickname by which some people called you in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Well, I have got some kind of a nickname, Prco.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. The Judges already heard about the location of various villages around Vitez, and they already heard about the population of the village, that is to say, how many Muslims and how many Croats there were. I imagine you know that there were some more Muslims than you Croats in the village, but that is a fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As we said a few minutes ago, Mr. Vinac, you're the father of four children; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your first child, Irena, was born in 1994 [as interpreted]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, on May 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your daughter was christened. Who was her first godmother?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: It was Kata Vinac, nee Skopljakovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your other child and your only son, Mario, was born on the 27th of October, 1985?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: That son was also christened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who were his godparents?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: The godparent was Marijan Ceko from Poculica, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is that the only godparent of the child?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. After your son Mario, your daughter Marija was born?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When was she born?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender a document now. This is just a birth certificate of this third daughter, Marija. It is from the Seti Juri [phoen] department in Vitez of the archbishop's office. This is a birth certificate for Marija Vinac.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the document in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, this is the birth certificate of your daughter, Marija. When was she christened? You have the original in front of you, so take a look.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: She was christened on the 11th of October, 1990, in Vitez. My daughter Marija's godparent was Mrs. Zeljka Santic, nee Papic. Fraulein Mikic christened the baby. That is to say, that was the priest who christened the baby on that 11th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to remind the Trial Chamber that it just so happened that this priest is one of the two friars who was killed in the monastery in Fojnica in 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your fourth child, Lucija, she was born after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes. My fourth child, my third daughter, was born on the 24th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And again her godmother?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Her godmother is Dragica Cosic from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a mistake in the transcript. I was referring to November 1993, not November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So now we've spoken about all of your children. I asked you about their respective birth dates and when they were christened. My question is the following: After your daughter Marija was christened in 1992 [sic], in 1993, you did not have any children who were supposed to be christened?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Was Mr. Kordic ever the godparent of any of your children or anybody's children?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Dario Kordic was never the godparent of any one of my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, was Mr. Kordic ever your guest at your house in the village of Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Kordic was never my guest, either in my home, nor in Donja Veceriska; at least, I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Since Mr. Kordic was a well-known person, had he ever been in a small village? Would you have to know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, had Mr. Kordic come to Donja Veceriska, I certainly would have known about it. I would have heard about it or something in that sense. But he was never there. At least, I never heard of it, nor did I ever see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Once again, we are making it quite difficult for the interpreters. Please don't answer my questions immediately. Just wait for a few moments before my question is interpreted. Very well. Mr. Vinac, your name was mentioned in this case even before you came here to testify. You know about Midhat Haskic's statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In it he claimed that on the 15th of April, 1993, in the cafe of one of the Drmic brothers -- one of them testified just before you did now -- you were together with Mr. Kordic and you were celebrating the christening of your child.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this piece of information is incorrect. On that day, the 15th of April, I was at work in Vitez, in the military district of Vitez then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of celebration at your home? He says that it was your son's birthday party.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on that day I was not in the cafe at all, nor was there any kind of celebration. I came home around 6.00 p.m., and I was not in the cafe. And on that day Mr. Kordic was not in Donja Veceriska at all, or was he ever there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
