utterances.text: So, in conclusion, were you, either on your own or with Mr. Kordic, in the cafe owned by the Drmic brothers in the Cafe Ravne in Donja Veceriska on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never with Mr. Dario Kordic in the cafe owned by the Drmic brothers, nor did I ever entertain as a guest Mr. Dario Kordic at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Since we're talking about Mr. Midhat Haskic already, I assume that he knew you. He was another person from the same village that you're from?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I knew Mr. Midhat Haskic. May he rest in peace. He is a dead man. I personally knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you know that he died?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he died, and he was buried in Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, when you said that you knew him, you knew him in all kinds of life situations; you lived alongside him for years. Could you tell us what he is like? Was he sick? Did he like to have a drink or two? Tell us anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew the late Mr. Midhat Haskic. He was a salesperson. He liked to have a drink or two when he would drink, he would like to tell some kind of stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What are you actually referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Well, when one has a drink or two, well, then he would add a few things to the truth. Again, I repeat, may God rest his soul.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, what is your conclusion, from your angle? Could he be trusted?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: From my angle, this is a falsehood, I mean the story he told, that Mr. Kordic was my -- was the godparent of one of my children and that he was in Donja Veceriska. So he was telling lies. This was nothing. It was just stories. Everybody in the village knew that he liked to talk a bit too much, and otherwise, as far as I know, he was a sick person. I think he had asthma. He had some kind of a lung problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Vinac: Quite a few inhabitants of Donja Veceriska share the same surname with you, and some are distantly related to you, others are closely related to you. I want to ask you about Dragan Vinac, who is distantly related to you. Do you know whether Dragan Vinac, or anyone else, for that matter, from the Vinac family, in the narrower or broader sense of the word, was ever Mr. Kordic's escort or driver, or do you know of any one of them having worked in Mr. Kordic's office in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no member of the Vinac family, including Dragan Vinac, was not the bodyguard or the driver of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my questioning. I wish to thank Mr. Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of what HVO unit were you a member?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I belonged, at the time, in February 1992 all the way up to June 1992, to the municipal staff; that is to say, I was attached to the defence department in Vitez. Then I was transferred to the military district of Vitez, that is to say, the Operative Zone before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard of various names of units based in Vitez. Which unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know of the name Vitezovi, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your connection to that unit or to its leader, Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my connection to the members of the unit was absolutely nonexistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the Viteska Brigade? What was your connection to that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I never had anything to do with that brigade, or was I a participant in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say that with equal force, do you, to what you've just said about the Vitezovi; you're definitely not a member of either group?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was neither a member of the Vitezovi or of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have another name as well as Mile? I don't mean a nickname. Do you have another given name apart from Mile?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I have a nickname. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but do you have -- I don't know. Is the naming system in your country such that you can have more than one given name, and if so, do you have a second given name?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. They're just nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've probably given it to us. What is your nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Well, it was Prco.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you were born in 1960?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And does the name Nike associate itself with you in any way, Mile Nike Vinac? Is that you?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is my father's name, Niko Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So therefore, Nike probably means "son of" or something like that, does it, and so your full name would indeed be Mile Nike Vinac?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will turn to that in a minute. What you're saying about the reliability of Mr. Midhat -- I want to deal with in a little more detail, Mr. Midhat Haskic. What are you saying about his telling of untruths, please? Don't feel embarrassed about the fact that he's a dead man. We all have to deal with these things. Say what you want to, full strength, about whether he told untruths.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Midhat Haskic spoke falsehoods. Whatever he said was false and untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forget the statement for the time being, that is, the statement that he made in relation to these matters. But generally around the village, just you tell us how far he went in telling untruths.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that man, wherever he went, he would, after a glass or two, tell all sorts of stories; not only around the village, all around throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Good-humoured stories about catching an oversize fish, or were they bad-humoured stories, telling bad gossip that wasn't true about people? I want the full picture, please, no holds barred.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, he said all sorts of things after a few glasses, all sorts of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let's break that down. It's only after a few glasses, is it, that this propensity to say things that weren't true could be detected?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: In a number of cases. But even without drinking, he was wont to say some untruths from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then let's have some examples. Don't worry about this statement. We'll come to that in a minute, in due course. Just you tell us some examples of what he said that was a tall story.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot recollect now exactly, but there were very many of them, and it was a long time ago. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, you've been brought here in order to help the Judges with an assessment, amongst other things, of the honesty of this man who is now dead, and you've told us, in your signed summary, that he was a well-known teller of improbable stories. That's the way you put it. I'd like one of the improbable stories, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot remember it now. It was a long time ago, and right at the moment I can't remember. I repeat it. Because I was personally offended and hurt by these lies, and Mr. Kordic too, because that was nothing but a lie, nothing but untruth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was offended, was he, by what Mr. Midhat Haskic said about him? Was he?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Listen. I don't know how everybody felt. That is how I felt, because that was nothing but a lie. It was a pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Kordic was also offended. Was he or wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat it. I do not know how other people felt, because I did not discuss it with Mr. Kordic. I did not talk about it with him at all. But I did feel hurt and offended, because that was sheer fabrication, sheer lie. And I've come here to tell the truth, and I solemnly declared that I would speak only the truth, and now Mr. Prosecutor is bringing pressure on me to admit to something that never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope I'm not putting any pressure on you except that which may be proper. You were the neighbour of Mr. Haskic for how many years?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we were neighbours ever since I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us that he had a habit of telling untrue stories. Did he tell them to you as you spoke across the garden fence, if there was a fence, or when you were outside the houses, coming and going? When did he tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've put the matter fully, Mr. Nice, on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, sometimes I heard it with my own ears, sometimes from other people, that he told untruths. And I repeat, I was personally hurt because that was a sheer lie, it was a fabrication and nothing but.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you on the night of the 15th/16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I was at home, in my own house in Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What time were you woken up on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I woke up around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard nothing in the way of unusual noises throughout the night?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: No, I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many metres from Midhat Haskic's house was your bedroom, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you mean as the crow flies or by road, because these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you were neighbours, it may not make much difference, but as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So if I've misunderstood it, you weren't immediate neighbours of this man -- no, no, I'm sorry, it's my mistake. I'll withdraw that question and come back to it in another way. On the 16th, what did you do on the day of the 16th and then on the evening of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't understand the question. Could it be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you do on the day of and the evening of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 15th of April, in the evening, I was at home, and sometime around 1900, I was watching television. I was watching massacred guys, Colonel Zivko Totic. And at sometime around 2100, I went to bed, and so did my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you heard nothing --

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I shall continue. There was a story going round the village that the Muslims and Croats might go to war, and when we saw that on television, those massacred young men, some of the population moved out towards Gornja Veceriska; I didn't, with my family, with my children. Sometime around 1.00, after midnight, I picked up the phone and I called the younger officer on duty at the military district, and I asked him about the situation in the area of responsibility because I knew that officer on duty, and he told me, "It's all quiet, no problem." So I went back to bed on the 15th of April. In the morning, however, around 7.00 I was woken up by detonations. First I did not react to several detonations, because in our village it was rather a custom for some to just throw something like that. But as the time went by, it was becoming ever louder, and I could see, when I came out, that there was a war raging all around me. Then I put my family into a motor vehicle, and I took my wife and my three children to the neighbouring village, because my fourth child was not born yet. And then I went back to defend my homestead. There was fighting during that day on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were part of the attack on the village by the Viteska Brigade; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, Your Honours. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You were a part of the HVO's attack on that village, and you were there probably as a member of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the HVO did not attack, nor do I know -- nor am I aware that it attacked the Muslims in Donja Veceriska, because when the gunfire began, I was asleep and I could not tell exactly who started the fire. But I assume, and that is what I heard from neighbours in my village, that it was the Muslims who were the first ones to open it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were injured on the 17th, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE VINAC
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honours. Not only was I lightly wounded next to my home, defending my home, but that day a projectile from a mortar blew to pieces my motor vehicle, as it was a direct hit, and my family house, from the western side, it damaged. It broke the window panes. And as I said, I remember how a mortar shell hit a pine near my house and simply split it into half. The projectiles were flying very high, so that the front of my family house was pretty well damaged. All the glass and all the window panes were gone, and the walls too were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know you said 10 past 4.00. I shan't be able to finish in just five minutes. I shan't be very much longer, but I've got a couple of documents I want to put to the witness which have only recently come to my attention, and if I could do it tomorrow morning, I could probably do it more tidily. I don't know if that, in those circumstances, would make this convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that would be convenient. Mr. Vinac, would you come back tomorrow, please, at half past nine in the morning to conclude your evidence. Would you remember, during the adjournment, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the Defence teams, and of course don't let any of them or anybody speak to you about your evidence. Half past nine tomorrow morning, please.
